clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive urea cycle disorder caused by deficiency of arginase 1, the final enzyme that hydrolyses arginine to ornithine and urea
Clinically atypical for a urea cycle defect, usually presenting after infancy rather than with an explosive neonatal hyperammonaemic crisis
The hallmark is a progressive spastic diplegia or tetraplegia, often initially mistaken for cerebral palsy
Developmental regression, cognitive decline, seizures and growth failure accompany the neurological picture
Plasma arginine is markedly elevated and is the key diagnostic clue, with guanidino compounds also raised
Hyperammonaemia tends to be milder and more episodic than in other urea cycle disorders, though crises can still occur
The progressive, worsening course distinguishes it from the static deficit of cerebral palsy
Management is generic: dietary protein and arginine restriction, essential amino acid support and ammonia scavenger therapy
reference.pathophysiology: Arginase 1 catalyses the terminal step of the urea cycle, splitting arginine into ornithine and urea and thereby both disposing of waste nitrogen and regenerating ornithine for the next cycle. Its deficiency causes accumulation of arginine and its guanidino metabolites, which are thought to be neurotoxic and to drive the characteristic progressive spasticity and cognitive decline. Because residual ureagenesis through other pathways is comparatively preserved, ammonia elevations are usually milder and intermittent rather than presenting as overwhelming neonatal hyperammonaemia. Chronic exposure to raised arginine and guanidino compounds, punctuated by episodic hyperammonaemia, underlies the clinical course.
additionalDifferentials: Cerebral palsy (spastic diplegia) of non-metabolic cause
Other urea cycle disorders such as OTC or citrullinaemia
Arginine:glycine amidinotransferase and other neurometabolic disorders
Leukodystrophies presenting with spasticity and regression
additionalInvestigations: Plasma amino acids showing markedly elevated arginine
Plasma ammonia, particularly during symptomatic episodes
Urinary orotic acid and guanidino compounds
Red cell or fibroblast arginase enzyme activity
Brain MRI to characterise white matter and other changes
redFlags: Acute hyperammonaemic encephalopathy with vomiting, lethargy or coma
Progressive spasticity and regression in a child previously labelled as cerebral palsy
New seizures with an unexplained rise in ammonia
Catabolic stress such as infection or fasting precipitating decompensation
reference.prognosis: Untreated disease is progressive with worsening spasticity and cognitive impairment, but early protein restriction, arginine limitation and scavenger therapy can slow or stabilise neurological deterioration and reduce hyperammonaemic episodes.
pitfalls: Diagnosing cerebral palsy and missing a treatable metabolic cause of progressive spasticity
Expecting a neonatal hyperammonaemic crisis and dismissing the diagnosis when it is absent
Giving arginine supplementation as used in some other urea cycle disorders, which is contraindicated here
Overlooking milder, episodic hyperammonaemia because ammonia is normal between crises
references: Summar ML et al. Urea cycle disorders overview
Blau N. Physician's Guide to the Diagnosis, Treatment, and Follow-up of Inherited Metabolic Diseases
